articles.standfirst: Justificativa para não votar deve ser feita pelo aplicativo e-Título ou diretamente em seções eleitorais.
articles.summary: Justificativa para não votar deve ser feita pelo aplicativo e-Título ou diretamente em seções eleitorais.
articles.body:
Quem pretende usar o e-Título no dia da eleição precisa atualizar o aplicativo — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução

Neste domingo (25), os brasileiros voltam às urnas para o segundo turno das eleições de 2026 . No entanto, quem não conseguir comparecer ao local de votação pode justificar a ausência sem sair de casa. O procedimento pode ser feito de forma digital, por meio dos canais oficiais da Justiça Eleitoral, como o aplicativo e-Título e o Autoatendimento Eleitoral.

Se o eleitor não puder comparecer à votação por estar fora do domicílio eleitoral ou por qualquer outro motivo, deverá justificar a ausência.

A justificativa é obrigatória para eleitores entre 18 e 70 anos que deixarem de votar. Quem faltar ao segundo turno, precisa apresentar uma justificativa para a ausência .

A justificativa pode ser feita no próprio dia da eleição ou, se isso não for possível, em até 60 dias após cada turno.

Como justificar o voto no dia da eleição

A forma mais simples é pelo aplicativo e-Título . O eleitor deve:

abrir o aplicativo e acessar a opção "Justificativa de ausência" ;

selecionar a eleição e o turno correspondente;

anexar documentos, se o sistema solicitar, como atestado médico ou comprovante de viagem;

guardar o código de acompanhamento para consultar posteriormente se a justificativa foi aceita.

Quem não conseguir fazer a justificativa no dia da votação ainda pode regularizar a situação em até 60 dias após o segundo turno . Veja as opções disponíveis:

Reprodução de tela do e-Título — Foto: Reprodução

preencha o formulário referente ao turno em que faltou;

anexe documentos que comprovem a impossibilidade de comparecer.

Reprodução de tela do TSE. — Foto: Reprodução/TSE

Pelo Autoatendimento Eleitoral (no site do TSE)

Também é possível fazer o procedimento pelo sistema da Justiça Eleitoral. O eleitor deve:

selecionar a opção de justificativa eleitoral;

anexar documentos que comprovem o motivo da ausência.

Print do formulário de Requerimento de Justificativa Eleitoral (RJE). — Foto: Reprodução/TSE

Pelo formulário Requerimento de Justificativa Eleitoral (RJE)

Outra alternativa é enviar o Requerimento de Justificativa Eleitoral (RJE) à zona eleitoral. Nesse caso, é necessário:

anexar cópia dos documentos comprobatórios;

encaminhar o pedido à zona eleitoral responsável.

Eleitores com domicílio eleitoral no Brasil que estiverem fora do país no dia da votação também podem justificar a ausência. O pedido pode ser feito:

em até 30 dias após o retorno ao Brasil .

A justificativa pode ser apresentada por qualquer uma das três opções explicadas acima: pelo e-Título, pelo Autoatendimento Eleitoral ou pelo formulário RJE.

É importante anexar documentos que comprovem a viagem, como passagens, cartões de embarque ou carimbos no passaporte .

Já brasileiros inscritos na Zona Eleitoral do Exterior (ZZ) , que votam apenas para presidente da República, também têm até 60 dias após cada turno para apresentar a justificativa caso não compareçam à votação.

Quem deixa de votar e não apresenta justificativa fica sujeito ao pagamento de multa eleitoral, que pode custar até R$ 3,51.

Além disso, enquanto a situação não for regularizada, o eleitor pode enfrentar restrições para obter a certidão de quitação eleitoral, documento exigido em situações como posse em cargo público, inscrição em concursos públicos e emissão de passaporte.

Se a ausência ocorrer em três eleições consecutivas , sem justificativa e sem pagamento das multas, o título de eleitor poderá ser cancelado. Cada turno é considerado uma eleição para esse cálculo.

articles.title: Nunes Marques vota em Brasília e acompanha abertura de seção | G1
articles.standfirst: Mais de 158 milhões de eleitores poderão voltar às urnas para a definição de uma das disputas à Presidência da República mais acirradas da história do país.
articles.summary: Nunes Marques vota em Brasília após conferir a zerésima, enquanto 158 milhões de eleitores decidem a Presidência no segundo turno das Eleições 2026.
articles.body:
O presidente do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), ministro Kassio Nunes Marques , acompanhou a abertura de sua seção eleitoral e votou logo em seguida na manhã deste domingo (25), em Brasília.

Desse total, mais de 136 milhões são obrigados a votar e pouco mais de 22 milhões podem votar se assim desejarem.

Presidente do TSE, ministro Kássio Nunes Marques vota no 2º turno — Foto: Reprodução/ TV Globo

O ministro chegou à seção eleitoral no Lago Sul, bairro da capital federal, antes mesmo das 8h, horário previsto para o início da votação.

Ele acompanhou a emissão da zerésima da seção — relatório oficial que comprova que não há nenhum voto pré-computado ou registrado no sistema de totalização e nas urnas eletrônicas antes do início da votação (veja no vídeo acima). Logo depois, perto da abertura da votação, concluiu o voto.

Nunes Marques nasceu em Teresina (PI), e permanece com domicílio eleitoral na cidade. No entanto, nas eleições deste ano, pediu voto em trânsito para votar em Brasília.

A abstenção no 1º turno ultrapassou a marca de 33 milhões de eleitores — 21,08% do eleitorado apto a votar — e atingiu o nível mais alto desde 1998.

Esse eleitor, que pode fazer a diferença, qualquer que seja o candidato, pode votar no segundo turno.

➡️ Para a Justiça Eleitoral, cada turno é um novo pleito e, portanto, faltar ao primeiro não impede que o eleitor vote no segundo.

articles.title: Presidente da República: o que faz, quanto ganha e requisitos | G1
articles.standfirst: Entenda quais são as funções do chefe maior do Poder Executivo nacional. O g1 detalha as atribuições de cada um dos cinco cargos em disputa no pleito de 2026.
articles.summary: Entenda quais são as funções do chefe maior do Poder Executivo nacional. O g1 detalha as atribuições de cada um dos cinco cargos em disputa no pleito de 2026.
articles.body:
Os cinco últimos presidentes do Brasil. — Foto: Palácio do Planalto/Divulgação

No segundo turno das eleições 2026 , Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) e Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) disputam a Presidência da República. O presidente é o chefe do Poder Executivo federal e a principal autoridade do país, eleito para um mandato de quatro anos, com possibilidade de uma reeleição consecutiva. Quem ocupa o cargo acumula duas funções:

chefe de Estado , representando o Brasil nas relações internacionais; e

chefe de Governo , responsável por administrar a máquina pública federal e coordenar as políticas nacionais .

Também cabe ao presidente comandar a administração federal. Ele nomeia e exonera ministros de Estado, escolhe dirigentes de órgãos e empresas públicas e define as prioridades do governo em áreas como economia, saúde, educação, segurança, infraestrutura e meio ambiente.

📅 O segundo turno das eleições de 2026, que definem o novo presidente do Brasil, acontecem neste domingo (25). A disputa é entre Lula (PT) e Flávio Bolsonaro (PL).

Também integram as atribuições do presidente:

indicar representantes diplomáticos do Brasil; e

escolher nomes para ocupar cargos de relevância nacional, como o Procurador-Geral da República e ministros do Supremo Tribunal Federal – ambos a serem validados pelo Senado.

Atualmente, o presidente da República recebe um subsídio mensal bruto de R$ 46.366,19. O valor é definido por lei e corresponde à remuneração mensal do cargo, sem gratificações ou adicionais. O presidente também tem direito a benefícios previstos para o exercício da função, como residência oficial e estrutura de apoio para atividades institucionais.

Além do salário, o presidente conta com uma estrutura custeada pelo governo federal para o desempenho das funções do cargo, incluindo segurança, transporte oficial e servidores de apoio.

Esses itens, porém, não são incorporados ao salário e não devem ser considerados como parte da remuneração mensal do presidente.

O presidente pode apresentar projetos de lei ao Congresso Nacional, além de sancionar ou vetar propostas aprovadas pela Câmara dos Deputados e pelo Senado .

Também pode editar medidas provisórias, que têm força de lei imediata, mas validade de 60 dias. Essas precisam passar pelo Congresso para continuarem em vigor.

Outra atribuição é elaborar o planejamento financeiro do governo federal.

O presidente envia ao Congresso o Plano Plurianual (PPA) , a Lei de Diretrizes Orçamentárias (LDO), e a Lei Orçamentária Anual (LOA) . As três tratam de regras e definem prioridades e gastos da União para curto e médio prazo.

Como chefe de Estado, o presidente representa o Brasil em encontros internacionais, negocia acordos e tratados com outros países e mantém relações diplomáticas. Em muitos casos, esses acordos também precisam da aprovação do Congresso Nacional.

Apesar de ocupar o cargo mais alto do Poder Executivo, o presidente não pode governar sozinho . Projetos de lei, mudanças na Constituição, criação de impostos e boa parte das medidas que envolvem gastos públicos dependem da aprovação da Câmara dos Deputados e do Senado.

Além disso, o Congresso pode derrubar vetos presidenciais e abrir processo de impeachment em caso de crime de responsabilidade . As decisões do presidente também estão sujeitas ao controle do Poder Judiciário, dentro do sistema de freios e contrapesos previsto pela Constituição.

O presidente também é o comandante em chefe das Forças Armadas . Ele define a política de defesa nacional, nomeia os comandantes da Marinha, do Exército e da Aeronáutica e pode autorizar o emprego das tropas nas situações previstas pela Constituição.

articles.title: Horário de votação nas eleições 2026 muda dependendo do estado; veja | G1
articles.standfirst: A diferença ocorre por causa dos fusos horários adotados em diferentes regiões do país e também afeta o encerramento das urnas.
articles.summary: A diferença ocorre por causa dos fusos horários adotados em diferentes regiões do país e também afeta o encerramento das urnas.
articles.body:
O horário de votação do segundo turno das eleições 2026 segue uma regra nacional, mas o relógio local não marcará a mesma hora em todo o país devido ao fuso horário de algumas regiões. Isso acontece porque a Justiça Eleitoral usa o horário de Brasília como referência para a abertura e o encerramento das urnas.

No horário de Brasília, as seções eleitorais funcionarão das 8h às 17h. Em estados que estão em fusos horários diferentes, porém, o eleitor deverá seguir o horário correspondente no relógio local.

A diferença é importante principalmente para quem vota no Acre, Amazonas, Mato Grosso, Mato Grosso do Sul, Rondônia e Roraima. No outro extremo, Fernando de Noronha, em Pernambuco, terá votação mais tarde no horário local.

Confira como fica o horário das urnas no dia da eleição, considerando o horário local:

Amazonas : das 7h às 16h na maior parte do estado;

Amazonas : das 6h às 15h em 11 municípios;

Fernando de Noronha (PE) : das 9h às 18h;

Demais estados e Distrito Federal : das 8h às 17h.

Os horários acima consideram o relógio local de cada região. A referência oficial da Justiça Eleitoral é o horário de Brasília.

No Acre, as urnas funcionarão das 6h às 15h no horário local.

Isso ocorre porque o estado está duas horas atrás de Brasília. Assim, quando forem 6h no Acre, serão 8h na capital federal, horário definido para o início da votação.

Que horas começa a votação em Mato Grosso, Mato Grosso do Sul, Rondônia e Roraima?

Nesses quatro estados, a votação ocorrerá das 7h às 16h no horário local.

A diferença é de uma hora em relação ao horário de Brasília. Portanto, 7h nesses estados corresponde a 8h em Brasília.

O Amazonas tem dois horários locais para a votação, porque o estado possui municípios em fusos diferentes.

Na maior parte do estado, as urnas funcionarão das 7h às 16h no horário local.

Já em 11 municípios , a votação será das 6h às 15h:

Que horas começa a votação em Fernando de Noronha?

Em Fernando de Noronha, distrito de Pernambuco, a votação ocorrerá das 9h às 18h no horário local.

O arquipélago está uma hora à frente de Brasília. Dessa forma, 9h em Fernando de Noronha corresponde a 8h no horário de Brasília.

articles.title: Eleições 2026: como votar em trânsito no segundo turno? | G1
articles.standfirst: Por essa modalidade, quem estiver fora da cidade onde vota em outubro poderá participar da eleição em outro ponto do país. O prazo para solicitar o voto em trânsito, porém, já terminou.
articles.summary: Por essa modalidade, quem estiver fora da cidade onde vota em outubro poderá participar da eleição em outro ponto do país.
articles.body:
Neste domingo (25), eleitores que optarem pelo voto em trânsito no segundo turno das Eleições 2026 poderão votar fora da cidade onde têm domicílio eleitoral. O prazo para solicitar a modalidade terminou em 20 de agosto.

A opção estará disponível nas capitais e em municípios com mais de 100 mil eleitores. Os locais de votação serão definidos pelos Tribunais Regionais Eleitorais (TREs).

Veja abaixo como funciona o voto em trânsito.

O voto em trânsito permite que cidadãos que estão fora da cidade onde votam participem da eleição em outro local.

A modalidade existe nas eleições gerais, quando são escolhidos presidente, governadores, senadores e deputados federais, estaduais e distritais.

A pessoa que estiver em cidades diferentes nos dois turnos da eleição pode solicitar a habilitação para votar em trânsito em uma cidade distinta em cada turno.

Após as eleições, o título retornará à seção eleitoral de origem automaticamente, o que dispensa a necessidade de pedir a transferência de volta ao domicílio eleitoral original.

Em quais cargos o eleitor pode votar nesta situação?

Isso depende de onde o eleitor estará no dia da votação. Quem estiver no mesmo estado, mas em outra cidade, pode votar para presidente da República, governador, senador, deputado federal e deputado estadual ou distrital.

Já quem estiver fora do estado onde vota poderá escolher apenas o presidente da República.

Como funciona para quem mora no exterior?

Brasileiros que moram no exterior e estarão no país durante as eleições também podem usar o voto em trânsito.

Quem tem título registrado no exterior pode votar no Brasil em outubro, desde que solicite o voto em trânsito no mesmo prazo para quem mora no Brasil.

O que acontece se o eleitor não comparecer?

O eleitor que se inscreveu para o voto em trânsito e não pôde comparecer deve justificar a ausência, mesmo que esteja na cidade onde tem inscrição eleitoral no dia da eleição.

articles.title: Por que demora para a urna confirmar? Entenda intervalo de conferência | G1
articles.standfirst: A tecla verde da urna eletrônica perde funcionalidade por 1 segundo para a conferência do voto. Pressionar a tecla 'Confirma' não anula o voto. Entenda processo antes de votar no segundo turno.
articles.summary: A tecla verde da urna eletrônica perde funcionalidade por 1 segundo para a conferência do voto. Pressionar a tecla 'Confirma' não anula o voto.
articles.body:
Urna eletrônica — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

Durante a votação do primeiro turno das Eleições 2026 , eleitores comentaram nas redes sociais que apertaram o botão "Confirma" duas vezes ao escolher o candidato .

Isso pode acontecer porque a urna eletrônica tem um intervalo de um segundo destinado à conferência do voto antes de liberar a tecla verde. Mas não afeta em nada o voto de cada eleitor (entenda abaixo antes de votar no segundo turno).

O recurso existe desde as Eleições 2022 e foi criado para estimular o eleitor a verificar os dados do candidato antes de concluir a votação.

Depois que todos os números da candidata ou do candidato são digitados, a mensagem "Confira seu voto" aparece no rodapé da tela da urna e pisca por um segundo. Durante esse intervalo, a tecla verde "Confirma" fica temporariamente inativa.

Por isso, se o eleitor apertar o botão nesse momento, nada acontece. Assim que o período de conferência termina, quem havia apertado o "Confirma" durante esse período teve que pressionar a tecla novamente para registrar o voto.

O voto não é anulado nem perdido caso a pessoa aperte "Confirma" enquanto a tecla ainda estiver bloqueada.

Segundo a Justiça Eleitoral, o intervalo foi implementado para dar mais tempo para que o eleitor confira as informações que aparecem na tela da urna antes de confirmar sua escolha.

o eleitor digita o número da candidata ou do candidato;

as informações correspondentes aparecem na tela;

a mensagem "Confira seu voto" é exibida no rodapé por um segundo;

nesse período, a tecla "Confirma" fica inativa;

depois do intervalo, o botão é liberado e o eleitor pode confirmar normalmente.

A Justiça Eleitoral alerta ainda para uma informação falsa que circula nas redes sociais sobre o funcionamento das urnas.

Publicações afirmam que seria necessário esperar a frase "Confirma o seu voto" aparecer na tela antes de apertar a tecla verde e que quem pressionasse o botão antes disso poderia perder o voto. A informação é falsa.

A frase "Confirma o seu voto" não aparece na urna eletrônica. A mensagem exibida pelo equipamento é "Confira seu voto".

Se a tecla verde for pressionada durante o segundo reservado à conferência, ela apenas não produzirá efeito. Depois que o botão for liberado, basta apertá-lo novamente para concluir o voto.

articles.title: Flávio Bolsonaro vota no Rio de Janeiro no 2º turno das eleições | G1
articles.standfirst: Seção do candidato do Partido Liberal (PL) fica na Escola Municipal Barão Homem de Mello.
articles.summary: O candidato Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) compareceu à Escola Municipal Barão Homem de Mello, na Zona Norte do Rio, para registrar seu voto no segundo turno das eleições.
articles.body:
O candidato à Presidência da República Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) votou no início da manhã deste domingo (25) no Rio de Janeiro .

Assim como no 1º turno , ele chegou pouco depois das 8h, logo após a abertura dos portões da Escola Municipal Barão Homem de Mello, em Vila Isabel, na Zona Norte. Flávio votou na seção 170.

Flávio estava acompanhado da mulher, Fernanda, e do governador eleito do RJ, Douglas Ruas ( PL ).

Flávio Bolsonaro , que terminou à frente no 1º turno, é o representante do bolsonarismo na disputa presidencial de 2026. Aos 45 anos, o senador pelo Rio de Janeiro é o filho mais velho do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro (PL) e foi escolhido como candidato do partido no fim de 2025, após disputas internas.

Durante a campanha, Flávio buscou se apresentar como herdeiro político do pai. Ele disputa o 2º turno com o atual presidente, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ( PT ).

Formado em Direito, Flávio iniciou a carreira política aos 21 anos e exerceu 4 mandatos como deputado estadual. Em 2016, concorreu à Prefeitura do Rio, mas não foi eleito.

Dois anos depois, recebeu mais de 4 milhões de votos e foi o candidato ao Senado mais votado no RJ. Atualmente, está no fim do mandato de senador.

articles.summary: Os dados podem ser consultados até o dia das eleições no portal do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral, nos sites dos tribunais regionais e no aplicativo e-Título.
articles.body:
Urna eletrônica exibida em evento do Tribunal Regional Eleitoral do Rio de Janeiro (TRE-RJ), no Rio — Foto: Tânia Rêgo/Agência Brasil

Quem vai votar no segundo turno das eleições de 2026, neste domingo (25), pode consultar o local de votação pela internet . A consulta é gratuita e pode ser feita pelos canais oficiais da Justiça Eleitoral, sem necessidade de comparecer ao cartório eleitoral.

Os dados estão disponíveis no Autoatendimento Eleitoral (Título Net) e no aplicativo e-Título (disponível na App Store e na Google Play) .

Pelo sistema, o eleitor pode descobrir onde vai votar nas eleições de 2026. Na opção "Onde votar", basta preencher os dados solicitados para visualizar:

Print da página do Autoatendimanto Eleitoral. — Foto: Reprodução

articles.title: Qual a diferença entre o primeiro e o segundo turno? | G1
articles.standfirst: O segundo turno ocorrerá neste domingo (25) e eleitores do Brasil inteiro deverão escolher seu candidato a presidente. Em cinco estados e no DF, haverá também votação para governador.
articles.summary: O segundo turno ocorrerá neste domingo (25) e eleitores do Brasil inteiro deverão escolher seu candidato a presidente. Em cinco estados e no DF, haverá votação para governador.
articles.body:
Urna eletrônica — Foto: Giuliano Gomes/PR Press

Neste domingo, 25 de outubro, os mais de 158 milhões de eleitores habilitados no Brasil voltarão às urnas eletrônicas para o segundo turno das eleições .

Enquanto o primeiro turno abrange a votação para cargos do legislativo (deputados estaduais, federais e senadores) e executivo (presidente e governadores), o segundo turno é destinado exclusivamente à escolha dos chefes do poder executivo.

De acordo com a Constituição Federal , há segundo turno para a disputa da prefeitura quando os candidatos não conseguem alcançar a maioria absoluta dos votos válidos no primeiro turno – ou seja, 50% mais um.

Nesse caso, disputam o segundo turno os dois concorrentes mais votados na primeira etapa.

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) e Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) disputam a cadeira de presidente. Além disso, apenas cinco estados e o Distrito Federal terão disputa de goverrnador em 2º turno. Quem mora nestes locais, portanto, devem votar em presidente e governador no dia 25:

Espírito Santo : Lorenzo Pazolini (Republicanos) e Ricardo Ferraço (MDB) vão disputar o 2º turno

Amazonas : Omar Aziz (PSD) e Professora Maria Do Carmo (PL) vão disputar o 2º turno

Rio Grande do Norte : Allyson (União) e Cadu De Lula (PT) vão disputar o 2º turno

Acre : Mailza Assis (Progressistas) e Alan Rick (Republicanos) vão disputar o 2º turno

Tocantins : Professora Dorinha (União) e Vicentinho Júnior (PSDB) vão disputar o 2º turno

Distrito Federal : Celina Leão (Progressistas) e Leandro Grass (PT) vão disputar o 2º turno

Para votar no segundo turno, o eleitor cumpre as mesmas regras que as observadas na primeira etapa da votação: é preciso ter em mãos documento original com foto, além de deixar o aparelho celular com o mesário antes de se dirigir à cabine de votação na sua zona e seção eleitoral.

Os eleitores podem conferir o local de votação no documento do título de eleitor, no aplicativo e-Título ou pelo 'Autoatendimento Eleitoral', no site do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), clicando na Onde votar e preenchendo os dados solicitados.

No site do TSE, é possível encontrar o local de votação. — Foto: Reprodução

IMPORTANTE: Os eleitores aptos que não votaram na primeira etapa de votação das Eleições Municipais de 2024, ocorrido em 6 de outubro, podem e devem participar do segundo turno .

A Justiça Eleitoral considera cada turno de votação uma eleição independente para efeito de comparecimento da eleitora ou do eleitor à urna eletrônica.

Ou seja: a ausência de comparecimento ao primeiro turno não impede os eleitores de exercerem o direito de voto na segunda etapa de votação.

articles.title: Eleições 2026: acompanhe a cobertura do 2º turno nas regiões de Bauru, Itapetininga, Presidente Prudente, Rio Preto e Sorocaba
articles.summary: Moradores do interior de SP voltam às urnas neste 2º turno das Eleições 2026 para escolher o presidente do Brasil; siga em tempo real.
articles.body:
Moradores do interior de SP voltam às urnas neste 2º turno das Eleições 2026 para escolher o presidente do Brasil; siga em tempo real.

O segundo turno das Eleições 2026 é realizado neste domingo (25);

Os eleitores do interior de SP voltam às urnas para definir quem será o novo presidente da República;

Estão na disputa os candidatos Flávio Bolsonaro, do PL, e Lula, do PT;

Com início às 8h em todo o país, os eleitores podem votar até as 17h.

Os eleitores de Macedônia (SP) também voltam às urnas neste domingo (25) para eleger o prefeito e o vice-prefeito em uma eleição suplementar . A votação será realizada em conjunto com o segundo turno das eleições presidenciais. Com isso, os moradores da cidade farão duas escolhas durante o pleito.

A gestão dos novos mandatários eleitos no município será iniciada em 1º de janeiro de 2027 e se estenderá até 31 de dezembro de 2028. Ao todo, 4.118 eleitores estão aptos a votar em Macedônia.

Os eleitores de Macedônia (SP) voltam às urnas neste domingo (25) para eleger o prefeito e o vice-prefeito em uma eleição suplementar. A votação será realizada em conjunto com o segundo turno das eleições presidenciais. Com isso, os moradores da cidade farão duas escolhas durante o pleito.

O temporal que atingiu a região de Itapetininga (SP) entre a noite deste sábado (24) e a madrugada deste domingo (25) provocou alagamentos, deslizamento de terra e deixou moradores desabrigados.

A Defesa Civil estadual mantém o alerta laranja para todo o estado de São Paulo neste domingo, devido à previsão de novas pancadas de chuva, que podem ser intensas e acompanhadas de raios, rajadas de vento e queda de granizo.

A circulação de trens da Linha 7-Rubi, que liga São Paulo a Jundiaí, está interrompida no trecho entre as estações Botujuru e Campo Limpo Paulista desde as 5h09 deste domingo (25). A operação entre Palmeiras-Barra Funda e Botujuru e entre Campo Limpo Paulista e Jundiaí segue normalmente. De acordo com a concessionária, para atender os passageiros, ônibus gratuitos do sistema PAESE foram acionados para cobrir o trecho afetado até que a circulação seja normalizada.

A TIC Trens informa que as equipes de manutenção atuam no local para restabelecer a operação no menor tempo possível e os passageiros estão sendo orientados por meio de avisos sonoros nos trens e nas estações, além do atendimento prestado pelos agentes de atendimento e segurança.

A Linha 7, bem como todo o sistema de trens metropolitanos, oferece gratuidade na cobrança de passagem neste domingo, das 6h às 20h.

A chuva que atingiu Sorocaba na noite de sábado (25) e durante a madrugada deste domingo (26), dia do segundo turno das Eleições 2026, provocou transtornos em diferentes pontos da cidade.

Houve registros de alagamentos, interdições de vias e queda de muro. Segundo o Cartório Eleitoral de Sorocaba informou à TV TEM, não há mudanças de local de votação, havendo adaptações nas próprias escolas por eventual falta de energia e infiltrações.

Um dos principais impactos foi a cheia do Rio Sorocaba, que levou à interdição da Avenida Dom Aguirre nas proximidades da Praça Lions e do bairro Santa Rosália.

Neste domingo (25), os eleitores de Martinópolis e Narandiba também vão às urnas para escolher prefeito e vice . A votação suplementar acontece após a cassação dos políticos eleitos em 2024.

A ordem de votação na urna eletrônica nas duas cidades será: primeiro o voto para presidente da República e, na sequência, o voto para prefeito. A tela exibirá as informações e a barra de progresso nessa ordem.

Começa agora a cobertura ao vivo do 2º turno das eleições nas regiões de Bauru, Itapetininga, Presidente Prudente, Rio Preto e Sorocaba (SP) .

Eleitores do interior de SP voltam às urnas neste domingo (25) para definir quem será o novo presidente da República. A votação começa às 8h em todo o país.

articles.title: Elections cannot produce change in Israel
articles.summary: Political change cannot come from within Israeli society. It can only come from the outside.
articles.body:
Throughout the Israeli election campaign, the focus has been on two “blocs” – one led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the other opposing him. To the outside observer, the “pro-Netanyahu” and “anti-Netanyahu” labels imply that there are two different visions for the country and that the policies of the next government will depend on which one wins the elections.

This assumption is not surprising. In countries across the world, different candidates offer different visions for their country during electoral races. But in Israel, and particularly as it pertains to the Palestinians, this cannot be further from the truth.

Foreign diplomats ask about the future of the mythical “two-state solution” and talk about reconstruction plans in Gaza. They assume that Netanyahu is the reason for the lack of progress. Without him, everything will change. We can only wish.

One would think that three years of genocide, pending war crimes indictments, rulings and pending cases at the International Court of Justice as well as the scores of reports documenting Israel’s atrocities would affect the Israeli election. One would assume that when taking to the polls, Israelis would be thinking of what they have done to Palestinians, what this will breed for the future and, even selfishly, what it means for them. But they will not.

Instead, the vast majority of them will vote for candidates who, like them, support the continued denial of freedom for the Palestinians, the continued colonisation of the West Bank, the continued destruction of Gaza, the continued genocide of Palestinians and the continued bombing of and theft of land from neighbouring sovereign nations.

All this is apparent in the slogans and the statements that the candidates have put forward themselves: those supporting Netanyahu have called for Gaza to be flattened, have wished for the occupied West Bank to be turned into Gaza and have proclaimed that there are no innocents among the Palestinians.

Their ads feature bulldozers tearing down Palestinian homes, Palestinians starving and Israeli bombs exploding in civilian areas, with candidates promising even more. “Occupy. Expel. Settle” is one slogan.

What about the opposition? Their positions do not differ. For example, Avigdor Liberman, a staunch Netanyahu rival, has also long maintained that there are “no innocents in Gaza”. He and members of his party have worked to block food from getting into Gaza and have openly called for the takeover of Lebanon.

Even members of the opposition, who are considered leftists, like Yair Golan, have criticised the international recognition of Palestine and support Israel’s illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank.

Not a single candidate from the opposition parties supports the establishment of a Palestinian state.

So, genocide and the “two-state solution” will not be on the ballot on October 27. Neither will Israel’s “forever wars”. Rather, the electoral battle will be over the details: whether the Haredim (ultra-Orthodox) Jews should participate in these wars and how much Palestinians should be punished.

In short, what this coming election may change in Israel is the face of the government, not the policy.

The question then is what kind of a society overwhelmingly votes for politicians who openly speak about their desire to commit war crimes? The answer lies in the fact that these crimes have become normalised in Israel, so commonplace that not advocating for them is odd.

Since the establishment of Israel on the ruins of Palestinian homes and through the ethnic cleansing of Palestinians, Israeli society has never faced consequences for its actions, whether those actions were land theft, killing, imprisonment, collective punishment or even genocide.

The message the world has sent to Israelis is that they are “in their right” and that all that is needed is even more violence against the Palestinians to get precisely what they want: Palestine without Palestinians.

So while foreign diplomats and their governments may be viewing the removal of Netanyahu as the solution, this would not resolve the central problem: the belief that Israelis have superior rights; that they can do as they wish to Palestinians and that no one can stop them.

For far too long, Israel has been told that it can do as it pleases and face no consequences internationally. Change will not come from within the country. It can only come from the outside in the form of consequences.

Sanctions, for example, could work. Wide-ranging sanctions that isolate Israel economically and politically and make clear to the Israelis that they do not have the exceptional right to commit atrocities without being held to account.

Regardless of which bloc wins the Israeli elections, the international community must change its policy of silence and accommodation. If not, I suspect that “Occupy. Expel. Settle” will not remain a campaign slogan. It will be a promise that both “blocs” will fulfil.

articles.title: Iran’s oil lifeline is drying up. The biggest pain may fall on ordinary citizens
articles.summary: Iran's floating oil inventory has fallen to zero as the U.S. naval blockade tightens, but the IRGC may be shielded while civilians bear the pain.
articles.body: Iran is approaching a financial reckoning as a U.S. naval blockade threatens to wipe out its seaborne crude oil revenues by mid-December — but the economic pain may fall more heavily on ordinary Iranians than on the military Washington is trying to constrain. Iran’s trackable floating oil inventory outside the U.S. blockade zone has fallen to zero, according to energy intelligence firm Kpler, which projects that Tehran's crude revenues could dry up by the middle of December as outstanding payments are settled. But the loss of oil revenue would not necessarily translate into an immediate military funding crisis. Tehran could shield military spending while cutting civilian programs, allowing inflation to erode purchasing power and drawing on alternative revenue sources. BESSENT SAYS IRAN WILL HAVE 'NOTHING LEFT TO TRADE' WITHIN TWO WEEKS AS OIL LIFELINE DRIES UP That complicates Washington's pressure campaign: The blockade may deprive Tehran of one of its biggest sources of cash without immediately starving the military and Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of the money they need to operate. Oil directly accounts for roughly 30% of Iran's government budget, according to Gregory Brew, a senior Iran and energy analyst at Eurasia Group, and Miad Maleki, an Iran sanctions and financial expert at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies. Iran entered the year expecting to export about 1.7 million barrels per day at roughly $54 per barrel, Brew said. Actual exports have fallen short of that target, though higher oil prices allowed Tehran to build some financial cushion. Maleki estimated that oil and refined petroleum products account for between 50% and 60% of regime revenue when indirect income is included. Still, the December deadline is not a date on which Iran suddenly runs out of money. "The December timeline is more of a cash flow kind of disruption, and not really a collapse state," Maleki told Fox News Digital. Tehran has so far allowed inflation and the weakening rial to absorb some of the pressure rather than abruptly stopping government salaries or allowing widespread shortages to develop. "The purchasing power of Iranians incrementally declines," Maleki said. Losing a revenue stream that covers roughly 30% of the government budget would nevertheless force increasingly difficult choices. Tehran can cut spending, borrow more or run larger deficits. Deeper cuts could hit subsidies, pensions and other government programs, while deficit spending risks fueling already high inflation. "There's already expectations that government spending next year is going to be greatly reduced," Brew said . "A bigger chunk of the budget is likely going to be met through borrowing and deficit spending, which is of course going to add to inflation." IRAN LOSES KEY ECONOMIC LIFELINE IN MIDDLE EAST THAT TRUMP'S SANCTIONS COULDN'T REACH AS DEADLOCK PERSISTS Military spending, however, could prove more resistant. "There is a broad expectation that non-military spending is going to be slashed significantly, while military spending is going to be maintained and might even increase because of the overall war footing that the Iranian regime has been put on," Brew said. Iran is already spending resources to rebuild missile production facilities and other military infrastructure, expand underground facilities and repair damage to its nuclear program, Brew said. Iran's armed forces also have a direct connection to the country's oil trade. US TARGETS CHINESE REFINERY IN SWEEPING IRAN OIL CRACKDOWN, SANCTIONS ‘SHADOW FLEET’ TANKERS The Treasury Department said last year that Tehran was allocating roughly 200,000 barrels of crude per day to its armed forces, with the value of planned allocations expected to exceed $10 billion annually. Military organizations can sell allocated oil abroad and use the proceeds themselves. Maleki said those sales have helped finance equipment, chemicals and weapons components and support Iran-backed groups including Hezbollah and Hamas. The IRGC also draws revenue from smuggling, black-market commerce and sanctions-evasion networks outside the formal state budget. Brew said its economic influence has expanded as sanctions have squeezed Iran's private economy. "If the IRGC is the single most important institution in the country, and if it largely benefits from sanctions and blockades and various forms of U.S. economic pressure, then there's a world in which it benefits from this new environment rather than being squeezed like the overall government budget," Brew said. Iran's oil squeeze has been months in the making. Tehran held roughly 135 million barrels of crude in floating storage before the war began in February, providing a stockpile it could continue selling after U.S. forces restricted new exports. That offshore inventory has now been exhausted. U.S. Central Command estimates the blockade has already denied Tehran at least $25 billion in oil revenue. Buyers of Iranian crude typically settle payments one to two months after delivery, creating the lag between the disappearance of Iran's floating inventory and Kpler's projected revenue cutoff in December. Even if that projection broadly holds, however, Iran is unlikely to stop earning money from hydrocarbons altogether. Smaller quantities of oil can still move overland by truck and rail and across the Caspian Sea, while refined petroleum and petrochemical products can travel through routes outside the seaborne crude trade targeted by the blockade. "While the amount of Iranian oil that can be tracked has fallen to zero, it's unlikely Iran's oil exports completely fall to nothing," Brew said. "The amount will likely be fairly small, but it won't be completely zeroed." Both experts said an agreement with Washington allowing Iranian tankers to resume leaving the Persian Gulf could reverse the trajectory . Without a deal or relaxation of the blockade, the financial pressure is expected to build into next year. The bigger test may arrive in March, when Iran begins its new fiscal year and must reconcile its spending plans with dramatically lower oil income. "There's going to be a fiscal squeeze, and there's going to be pressure around the release of the new budget," Brew said. "There's going to be economic unrest, potentially even economic turmoil as the government rolls out spending cuts." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP By then, Tehran could have gone months without its traditional seaborne crude income, forcing the regime to decide how much of the financial squeeze it is willing to pass on to its population while preserving spending elsewhere.

articles.title: Leavitt says Trump is defying midterm headwinds as he barnstorms country
articles.summary: Karoline Leavitt reveals Trump's blunt strategy to combat negative approval ratings and rally MAGA voters who typically skip midterm cycles.
articles.body: MANCHESTER, N.H. - Former White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt says President Donald Trump is determined to defy a challenging midterm political landscape as Republicans fight to defend their narrow majorities in the House and Senate. "The president is defiant, and he always is optimistic," Leavitt said this week in a Fox News Digital interview in her home state of New Hampshire. The GOP is fighting political history, as the party in power in Washington has traditionally lost seats during midterm election years. Republicans also face a challenging campaign climate fueled by persistent inflation Americans see at the grocery store, high gas prices tied to what polls show is an unpopular war with Iran and Trump's increasingly negative approval ratings. KAROLINE LEAVITT SAYS TRUMP NEEDS A 'FIGHTER' AS SHE WEIGHS IN ON HER SUCCESSOR'S QUICK DEPARTURE Leavitt said Trump "totally understands that history is not on the Republican side right now if you just frankly look at the history books, but that's not stopping him from going out and barnstorming the country. He's been everywhere this week from North Carolina to South Carolina. Be in Michigan again this weekend." Republicans are also facing a low propensity problem in the midterms - MAGA supporters who don't always vote when Trump isn't on the ballot. "The president is getting out there and reminding voters what's at stake in this election and why it's so important to get out and vote in the midterms," Leavitt noted. "He's being frank and honest with his voters that 'I know you don't turn out in midterm cycles, but we need you to this time." Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin said recently in a social media post. "They are increasingly spending more and more money in the reddest of red areas in an attempt to hold on. We have them on the run - all gas, no brakes." DEMOCRACY 2026: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB But Leavitt, taking a page from the GOP midterm playbook, argued that "this election is a contrast between, between commonsense Republican conservative candidates who believe in cutting taxes, securing the border, putting American citizens over illegal aliens, and radical extreme liberal crazy candidates, some of the most radical Democrats we've ever seen run in the history of our country." articles.title: Alarming fraud trend puts small-town mosque with industry and foreign govt ties in focus: ‘Our motherland now’
articles.summary: Fox News Digital found Uzbek trucking companies donated hundreds of thousands to the Islamic Center of Maineville despite serious safety violations.
articles.body: This article is Part 2 of a Fox News Digital exclusive series investigating trucking fraud, public safety, and assimilation concerns in southwest Ohio. You can read Part 1 here. MAINEVILLE, OHIO — A mosque rising amid rural homes and farmland in southwest Ohio has become a focal point in the community’s growing concerns over an influx of foreign-owned trucking companies and trucking fraud, with a Fox News Digital review revealing significant financial ties between the mosque, trucking companies and the government of Uzbekistan. Roughly one mile north of the main intersection in Maineville, a small Warren County village with about 1,400 residents, sits the Islamic Center of Maineville, which has been under construction for the past four years following its approval by Hamilton Township in April 2022. Fox News Digital found that the mosque received substantial donations from trucking companies that government records show were cited for serious safety and compliance violations, while the mosque’s own Telegram channel displayed associations with people identified as current or former Uzbek officials. For years, the Islamic Center of Maineville has posted on Telegram to its 3,600 members, courting donations, acknowledging partnerships with trucking companies, and even sharing screenshots of donations from local trucking companies, owned by Uzbeks, totaling hundreds of thousands of dollars. HOW AN UZBEK TRUCK DRIVER’S FATAL CRASH EXPOSED TROUBLING FRAUD TREND IN MIDDLE AMERICA: ‘CHAMELEON CARRIERS’ Buraq Limited, a Springboro trucking company associated with Rukhshona Sultonova, donated at least $28,000 to the Islamic Center across 28 gifts, according to Telegram screenshots reviewed by Fox News Digital. A review of the company’s records found dozens of reported violations, including multiple English-proficiency violations, four ELD (electronic logging device) violations, three invalid-CDL violations, four expired medical cards and four hours-of-service violations. Premier Trucking Group Inc., owned by Sam Avazov, has received over 100 total violations, including for unsafe driving and invalid CDLs. In September, the Islamic Center posted a screenshot of a $1,000 donation from Premier Trucking Group, which has donated at least $25,000 to the mosque. OUT OF CONTROL, UNQUALIFIED ILLEGAL ALIEN TRUCKERS ENDANGERING KIDS ON US ROADS, INSIDER WARNS: ‘JUST MADNESS’ Foko Logistics LLC, owned by Abubakr Olimov and based in Hilliard, donated $20,000 in a single gift to the mosque, and had 52 violations across 37 inspections in FMCSA’s current 24-month record. The company had vehicle-maintenance violations involving damaged brake hoses, an inoperable tractor-protection valve and severely underinflated tires. Ten of its 24 vehicle inspections resulted in an out-of-service designation, a rate of 41.7%. Maca Transportation and Services LLC, based in Dayton and owned by Muminkhuja Kholkhujaev, donated at least $7,000 across eight gifts. FMCSA’s records show 120 violations across 72 inspections, including an English-proficiency failure and multiple false or incomplete hours-of-service records. The company also had serious brake, tire, and other vehicle-maintenance violations, with 14 of 36 vehicle inspections resulting in an out-of-service designation, or 38.9%. One trucking company that gave $150,000 to the mosque and helped organize the overall fundraising effort , Phoenix Cargo, told Fox News Digital the mosque approached the company multiple times asking for donations but said the $150,000 figure the company ultimately donated "represents only a fraction of the mosque's total construction budget" and that "Phoenix Cargo is not even among the project's top 100 donors." Phoenix Cargo has been cited hundreds of times for safety violations, including English proficiency, ELD tampering, and unsafe driving violations. Fox News Digital reached out to the mosque for comment but did not receive a response. Earlier this month, the Islamic Center said it is "committed to operating responsibly and in accordance with applicable law." "The fundraising for the Islamic Center concerns me because a large percentage of the Uzbek truck companies that donate have been repeatedly cited for the same kinds of serious inspection violations," Nodawolf, an online researcher who lives in the area and has been documenting alleged trucking fraud in southwest Ohio for months and was granted anonymity due to death threats he's received, said. "Those violations suggest a pattern of non-compliance with our laws and regulations among the donors, which is troubling given the community’s concentration in the freight industry in Maineville." Fox News Digital also asked the mosque if an administrator for their Telegram channel with the name "Bek A" is Bekhzod Asrarov, an Uzbek truck driver living in Maineville who authorities say struck and killed 21-year-old Ohio soccer player Tobias "Toby" Forsythe earlier this year. Asrarov was unable to communicate effectively in English at the scene, according to authorities, and has been accused of removing and concealing his dashcam after the crash. ICE LAUNCHES CDL FRAUD TIPLINE AS DHS HIGHLIGHTS DEADLY CRASHES INVOLVING ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS The mosque did not provide a response. The Islamic Center’s website says it does "not solicit donations from any foreign government, organization, association, partnership or individual or any agent thereof" and that "any such attempt" should be reported to the mosque immediately. However, the organization's Telegram account suggests close ties with the government of Uzbekistan, specifically when it comes to trucking companies. Hamkor Uz Cincinnati Association is a nonprofit organization established in 2020 to unite Uzbeks in the Cincinnati area and support community projects, including the construction of religious and cultural centers. Hamilton Township records identify Hamkor as the owner of the roughly 6.7-acre property where the Islamic Center of Maineville is being built. Telegram screenshots reviewed by Fox News Digital show the organization’s ties to former Uzbek government officials. One image shows the Mason office of Erkinbay Abdulla, with an accompanying message describing him as a former Uzbek official who "creates the trucking companies." Another screenshot contains a community statement attributed to Sukhrob Norbekov, whom an accompanying message identifies as another former Uzbek official who represents the mosque. The material places officials linked to Uzbekistan alongside an organization involved in the mosque project and individuals involved in creating local trucking companies. Current Uzbek officials also appear to be involved with the mosque and local trucking industry via the central Asian nation’s Ministry of Digital Technologies, according to photos posted on the mosque’s Telegram. The screenshots show a list of a six-member Uzbek delegation that traveled to the United States in April 2025, including Ambassador Furqat Sidiqov, regional government officials, and three officials from the Ministry of Digital Technologies. Separate posts invite entrepreneurs and truck-company managers to an April 19 IT conference hosted by Hamkor Uz Cincinnati at a banquet hall in Loveland, Ohio. TRUMP ADMIN INVESTIGATING 75 TRUCK DRIVER SCHOOLS FOR FRAUD, HELPING NON-CITIZENS GET LICENSES Additionally, a review of the Hamkor Uz Telegram channel, with current and former Uzbek government officials as administrators, showed advertisements for local trucking companies, removable truck signs, English courses for truck driving school, and legal counseling. Other posts include the owner of the mosque providing guidance on how to understand "Shariah compliant banking" and a post on "speaking English with the police" and how to "learn on the road." Nodawolf said the ties to the government of Uzbekistan are troubling to him "because these Uzbek trucking companies appear to be tightly organized, with patterns that look almost like a shared blueprint." "Given the documented safety and compliance problems in many of these companies, it’s reasonable to ask whether gaps in U.S. regulations are being systematically exploited," he added. Several locals who spoke to Fox News Digital said they have expressed their concerns about the rise in Uzbek trucking companies and potential safety gaps that could come along with it to their elected officials but have largely been ignored. "They're scared, I think they recognize that they could be called names, they can recognize they could be called out for, you know, like, Islamophobic or racist or things, but it's not that at all," a resident from nearby Middletown, Ohio, which has also experienced an influx of foreign-owned trucking companies, who posts information about trucking companies online under the name GHOSTOPSUZ, told Fox News Digital. One lawmaker who has taken action against trucking fraud is Ohio Republican state Rep. Michelle Teska, who represents most of Warren County, including Maineville, and has introduced legislation to strengthen commercial-driver licensing requirements, including a measure requiring driver examinations to be administered in English, which she told Fox News Digital addresses the "low-hanging fruit of the problem." "I did some research and basically found out that you can get your driver's license and your CDL license in the state of Ohio and you can have that test in 10 different languages," Teska said. "So that, to me, common sense says that's insanity." Teska says she has seen the problem "firsthand" while driving around her district, calling it "rampant." "This past weekend, I was at an event in Warren County and I was at an event that is right across the street from the BMV and I was just kind of observing a gentleman pulling in a semi truck cab into the parking lot on a Saturday at the BMV taking up four spaces, clearly had no idea how to drive the truck," Teska explained. "So I walked over to the BMV and spoke to this person and kind of confronted him and said, hey, do you speak English? He replied, no, I don't speak English. Asked him where he was from. He was from Uzbekistan. So it was crazy because I was watching it all take place live." Authorities in Warren County have been ramping up their presence in the trucking industry and on the roads in recent weeks, including a crackdown over the last week. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "The Hamilton Township Police Department actively monitors traffic safety concerns within our jurisdiction and works with our public safety partners to address violations and unsafe driving behaviors when identified," a spokesperson for Hamilton Township said. "In fact, our officers recently participated in a targeted traffic enforcement initiative focused on commercial motor vehicles, working alongside partner agencies to identify safety violations and improve roadway safety. We will continue to enforce applicable laws and take appropriate action when circumstances warrant." Warren County Prosecutor David Fornshell stressed there is nothing inherently wrong with mosque fundraising and he has not received any information that any laws have been broken. He told Fox News Digital, however, that clearly "there’s something going on" within the Uzbek community in southwest Ohio that "warrants at least awareness on the part of law enforcement." "It's disproportionate to what we see with any other immigrant community," Fornshell said. Since 2021, Fornshell said the area has seen an "influx of cases involving Uzbeks" that has prompted the need to hire more court interpreters and city employees who speak the language, particularly in the lower courts that deal with traffic offenses. "I would say hardly a week goes by where we don't have some felony case involving an Uzbek, it's pretty frequent at this point," Fornshell said. Census data from 2024 shows that roughly 1,500 people born in Uzbekistan live in Greater Cincinnati, while about 3,800 Uzbekistan-born residents live across Ohio. Uzbek community leaders say the actual population is significantly higher, estimating that roughly 4,000 Uzbek families live in southern Ohio, including U.S.-born children. "This is our motherland now, from now on," Hamkor Uz board member Nodirjon Ernazarov told the Cincinnati Enquirer through a translator last week in a story highlighting the Uzbek population’s efforts to become part of the community. The article explains that the influx of Uzbeks was driven, in part, by the area’s proximity to the trucking industry. "Uzbek people are very hardworking people," Ernazarov added. "So this mosque is (being built) by the help of all Uzbeks." The article does not mention that Ernazarov also owns a trucking company, Ray Cargo Corp., which has donated tens of thousands of dollars to the mosque and has been cited for numerous safety violations, including unsafe driving and driver fitness. Fox News Digital reached out to every trucking company mentioned in the article for comment.

articles.title: 7 nastiest moments of a mean campaign season
articles.summary: Election season is known for fiery policy exchanges and personal attacks, but November’s midterms have been marked by notable moments that have been criticized for going beyond the pale. From a controversial campaign ad in Ohio to a candidate telling his opponent to “shut up” on the debate stage, closely contested battleground races have become…
articles.body:
Election season is known for fiery policy exchanges and personal attacks, but November’s midterms have been marked by notable moments that have been criticized for going beyond the pale.

From a controversial campaign ad in Ohio to a candidate telling his opponent to “shut up” on the debate stage, closely contested battleground races have become ripe territory for a wave of vicious attacks on candidates’ characters.

Here are seven notable attacks from this election cycle.

GOP ad features opponent’s estranged mother

Ohio GOP gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy made headlines after his campaign released an advertisement featuring his opponent’s estranged mother.

In the video, Democratic candidate Amy Acton’s biological mother, Donna Arthur, called her daughter a “liar” and urged Ohioans to vote against her this November.

Philip Stearns, Acton’s brother, slammed the video as a “despicable low” for Ramaswamy’s campaign. The Democratic nominee previously disclosed in a 2019 interview that she suffered sexual abuse from her stepfather after her parents separated and that her mother stood by her abuser.

Ramaswamy’s campaign stood by the video amid criticism from Democrats and some Republicans, including Ohio Sen . Jon Husted and South Carolina Rep . Nancy Mace.

President Trump, meanwhile, doubled down in his support for Ramaswamy and the add, saying the Republican “should keep it up” while criticizing Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine’s (R) call to take it down.

Vice President Vance also defended the GOP candidate at a press conference last week.

“I have to admit that I’m a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America,” he said.

Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff has repeatedly called his opponent, GOP Rep. Mike Collins (Ga.), a “bigot” over past social media posts made by the congressman and his staff and family members.

On the debate stage in Atlanta earlier this month, Ossoff claimed Collins “hired half the Third Reich” to his congressional office and accused him of platforming “neo-Nazi content online.”

The Georgia Republican has faced scrutiny over social media posts made by his son-in-law and a former staffer that contained antisemitic messages.

The GOP senator responded to a moderator’s question about his son-in-law’s posts, saying he “condemned racism, anti-Semitism, hate.”

“I don’t care where the source is, and I tell him that too,” Collins said. “It’s wrong.”

Additionally, Ossoff and other Democrats have raised concerns with Collins’ own digital footprint, including a video he reshared from the University of Mississippi’s campus in 2024, which showed a Black woman surrounded by white students who are mimicking ape-like motions and making monkey sounds.

Collins captioned the post, “Ole Miss taking care of business.” He later acknowledged the video displayed “potentially inappropriate behavior that none of us should seek to glorify.”

“If John Lewis were marching today from Selma to Montgomery, Mike Collins would be grabbing a billy club,” the Georgia senator said on the debate stage.

Texas Democrat faces attacks on masculinity

Texas Senate nominee James Talarico (D) has been the subject of a series of attacks from the GOP regarding his masculinity and past veganism with nicknames like “low T Talarico” and “Tofu Talarico.”

Trump aide Stephen Miller suggested the Texas Democrat was transgender in a May social media post, while Vice President JD Vance insinuated the candidate was gay.

Vance made the remark in response to a rallygoer at a recent political event in Tyler, Texas.

“I love you too, sir. In a totally platonic way, to be clear. I’m the Vice President, not James Talarico,” he said.

While some Democrats have bristled at the many monikers the president has bestowed upon political adversaries, Talarico embraced Trump’s “Talafreako” brand.

“I call him Talafreako … because he is,” the president told Fox News’s Laura Ingraham. “He’s a freaky guy. He’s got something wrong with him.”

The Texas Democrat turned the viral attack into a fundraising opportunity, selling shirts on his campaign website that say, “I’m a Talafreako.”

“We’re grateful for the president for the nickname,” Talarico said to Jimmy Kimmel, telling the late-night host that the shirts were the “fastest selling item” on his campaign site.

Maine Democrat tells opponent: ‘Shut up’

Tensions boiled over at the Maine Senate debate on Oct. 15 when Democratic candidate Troy Jackson told his opponent, GOP incumbent Sen. Susan Collins, to “shut up.”

After an anti-data center protester interrupted the Republican lawmaker’s remarks, Collins suggested the heckler was “obviously one of Troy’s supporters.”

“Oh, shut up. I don’t even know that kid,” Jackson replied.

Maine’s Republican Party condemned the comment as “unacceptable behavior.” Collins told Fox News’s Sean Hannity the comment “didn’t surprise me,” referencing a 40-year-old allegation that Jackson pushed his longtime romantic partner, which both he and his partner have denied.

The Democrat doubled down on his comment when asked by CNN’s Dana Bash whether he regretted it.

“No, you know, she said that it was a Troy supporter. I mean, she accused me of setting that up. I had no idea who it was,” he said, adding he refused to be “accused of things like that.”

Trump repeatedly used an anti-transgender slur in a Truth Social post earlier this month to describe the Democratic candidate in South Carolina’s closely-contested Senate race.

Pediatrician Annie Andrews is challenging Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.), the president’s pick in this midterm contest.

In his post, the president praised Graham as a “High Quality person” before adding that her opponent was “not,” using the anti-transgender slur that rhymes with Andrews’s first name.

Trump went on to claim, without evidence, that the Democratic candidate was “in favor of Transgender for Everyone.”

Andrews brushed off the attack and said she was focused on lowering costs in the state in a statement to The Hill at the time.

“If you care more about your bills than the politics in Washington, this campaign is for you,” she said.

Muslim Brotherhood accusations in Michigan

The Republican nominee in Michigan’s tight Senate race, former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.), has repeatedly attempted to tie his Muslim opponent, Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed, to the Muslim Brotherhood.

Rogers has pointed to political donations to El-Sayed’s campaign from individuals connected to this Islamist group and claimed the Democrat has “ pledged his support ” to the organization, which the Trump administration designated as a terrorist group last year.

The Michigan-born Democrat has disavowed the group and said he was “proud to be an American” when asked about Rogers’s accusations during a Wednesday debate.

“I’m proud of our Constitution that guarantees all of us the right to pray as we choose to pray,” he continued. “And the question that you would ask that, I think, is actually really quite shameful.”

Additionally, Rogers drew criticism after he appeared to suggest during another debate earlier this month that El-Sayed could have terrorist relatives when discussing his position on guardrails for Flock cameras.

“Those programs were really, really important in catching people who were suspected … of committing a terrorist act, that’s really, really important,” Roger said. “And why would that bother you? Well, if someone in your family that might be on —”

El-Sayed cut him off, interjecting: “Go ahead and say it. You’ve been tiptoeing around it the whole time, just say it.”

Democrat faces online mockery over voice, appearance

Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens received a swarm of online mockery for a viral pep talk she gave to supporters ahead of Michigan’s Senate primary earlier this year.

Her opponent, El-Sayed, also faced accusations of sexism after he suggested in an interview with Semafor that the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), a major donor to Stevens’s campaign, should “find some way to teach her how to string together two coherent sentences.”

Sen. Gary Peters (D-Mich.), who is retiring from the contested Senate seat, accused supporters of El-Sayed who attacked the House Democrat’s appearance and voice of taking the “low road.” Peters backed Stevens in the Democratic primary.

In July, El-Sayed urged his supporters to “focus on the issues” in a statement shared on social media .

“It’s become impossible to ignore the way that people online make fun of my opponent for things that have nothing to do with her policies or politics,” he wrote. “It’s unkind and unhelpful. If you support me, please stop.”

El-Sayed went on to clinch the Democratic nomination in this race, with Stevens throwing her support behind him.

articles.body:
The Supreme Court is already confronting President Trump’s agenda this term, but a lot more is still coming.

The administration is petitioning the justices to take up 13 additional cases, The Hill’s analysis of the court’s docket shows.

Unlike lower courts, the justices choose which cases they hear. They’re still taking up cases for this term, meaning the battles could be resolved as soon as next year.

From transgender troops to an asylum ban, from foreign student deportations to horseracing, here’s where the Supreme Court could soon get involved.

Most immediately, the Supreme Court will turn to Trump’s Day 1 proclamation shutting down asylum processing at the southern border.

The American Civil Liberties Union convinced lower courts that Trump has exceeded federal law.

The administration’s appeal is on the justices’ list for their closed-door meeting on Friday. Trump’s proclamation remains in effect until they announce whether they’re taking it up.

Solicitor General D. John Sauer called it one of Trump’s “most important policy initiatives.”

The Trump administration’s ban on transgender troops serving openly in the military is back before the justices.

Last year, the Supreme Court issued an emergency ruling temporarily lifting a Seattle-based judge’s block on the ban. The battle has now returned for a final ruling, this time in a separate lawsuit filed in the nation’s capital.

A lower court told the Pentagon it can only enforce its ban against new recruits, not anyone already serving.

“That gravely erroneous holding warrants this Court’s review,” Sauer wrote to the justices. “The authority of the U.S. military to determine who may serve in the Nation’s armed forces is a matter of exceptional importance.”

The administration’s crackdown on pro-Palestinian foreign college students has arrived at the Supreme Court’s doorstep.

The Justice Department had already been urging the justices to take up its appeal concerning Badar Khan Suri , an Indian national and Georgetown University postdoctoral scholar whom the administration has tried to deport, when Mahmoud Khalil brought an appeal to the court this past week .

Khalil became a flashpoint in the crackdown as the administration looked to similarly deport the Columbia University demonstrator.

Lower courts have split on whether people in Suri and Khalil’s circumstances must wait for their immigration proceedings to conclude before trying to press a First Amendment defense in federal court.

The Trump administration contends that’s what federal law requires, but the duo say that unfairly leaves them open to mistreatment. In the lower courts, Suri won and Khalil lost.

“That is all practically disastrous,” Sauer told the justices. “The existing circuit conflict threatens intolerable disuniformity.”

The administration has appealed a decision siding with six University of California (UC) faculty and researchers, who sued after the administration terminated their federal grants.

The terminations came as part of Trump’s executive orders targeting diversity programs. The researchers say targeting them in that way violates their First Amendment free speech rights. Lower courts agreed, leading Sauer to petition the justices to get involved. He said the case is much bigger than the millions of dollars at stake for UC.

Sauer said it sets a “dangerous precedent that will hamstring every future administration when seeking to subsidize private projects that promote viewpoints aligned with government policy.”

The Trump administration has brought its attempts to install top federal prosecutors in offices across the country without Senate approval to the Supreme Court in two separate cases.

The first involves Sigal Chattah, whom the president wants to lead the U.S. attorney’s office in Nevada. The second involves John Sarcone, designated for the Northern District of New York.

After Trump took office, the Justice Department appointed them to lead the offices in an interim capacity. Federal law only allowed them to do so for 120 days, however.

At issue is what happened when the clock expired. The Justice Department has tried to keep Chattah and Sarcone atop their offices by designating them as their offices’ No. 2 official — called the “first assistant.”

Since no one is in the No. 1 spot, they automatically assumed the leadership responsibilities. Lower courts found that improperly sidestepped the confirmation process.

“Those holdings misconstrue the text and structure of the statute,” Sauer wrote to the justices. “They upend a quarter-century of practice. They threaten chaos for the next presidential transition.”

In 2025, the Supreme Court voted 6-3 to claw back judges’ ability to block the president’s policies nationwide. However, that decision left the door open to nationwide rulings in certain circumstances.

The administration now wants the justices to slam it shut.

At issue is the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), a federal law that tells judges to “set aside” an agency’s action when found to be arbitrary and capricious, unconstitutional or otherwise defective.

Judges have long interpreted that language to mean they should strike down a policy nationwide, not just grant relief to the plaintiffs before them.

“This Court should return the lower courts to their proper role,” Sauer wrote in the administration’s petition .

But this round, the president faces a steeper climb .

When the Biden administration tried advancing the argument several years ago, Chief Justice John Roberts slapped it down as “fairly radical.” Justice Brett Kavanaugh called it “far-reaching.”

This month, the Supreme Court was set to hear a case over whether it’s unconstitutional to deny a migrant a bond hearing when their detention becomes prolonged.

The argument never happened. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) pardoned the individual at the center of the case, and it became moot.

The same issue is back again at the Supreme Court with a different person’s case.

“The Court should likewise grant certiorari before judgment in this case as a replacement,” Sauer wrote in the government’s new petition .

The remainder of the administrations’ petitions don’t relate to Trump’s second-term agenda.

The justices are set to confront a bipartisan law Congress passed in 2020 overhauling horse track regulations, an attempt to implement national anti-doping standards to replace a patchwork of state rules.

Some Republican-led states and industry groups have challenged the scheme. They say it unconstitutionally hands over power to a private organization to help create those new standards.

At a previous stage of the case, the Supreme Court sided with the federal government . Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the only one to publicly dissent.

Now, the case has now returned to the justices’ normal docket.

Administrations in both parties have defended the law by emphasizing the government can reject the private group’s decisions.

“The Constitution allows executive agencies to receive such advice from private actors,” Sauer wrote .

The administration seeks review of a ruling that it illegally traded land formerly part of the Fort Hall Reservation to an agriculture company.

A lower court agreed it violated a 126-year-old law restricting the land, located in southeastern Idaho, siding with the tribes that live in the area.

“The decision below also needlessly complicates all federal land disposals,” Sauer warned .

Already, the court this term will hear a case asking whether federal law allows an immigrant to collect attorney’s fees when they successfully contested their immigration detention via what is known as a habeas petition.

The Trump administration, which argues they can’t, raises the same issue in two new cases . It told the justices they should just hold them until reaching their decision.

A similar dynamic is playing out in a man’s excessive force suit against federal agents who arrested him in a New Hampshire parking lot in 2016.

Fifty-five years ago, the Supreme Court ruled that someone whose constitutional rights are violated can, in certain circumstances, put the individual federal official on the hook for damages. It’s known as a Bivens claim.

Ever since, the justices have sharply limited when those suits are allowed.

They’ll hear arguments on the latest attempt next month. Now, the administration is bringing yet another case.

“At a minimum, the Court should hold the petition,” Sauer wrote.
