articles.title: Inside the Pentagon's doomsday plan to keep America fighting if global war erupts
articles.summary: The Pentagon's FORTRESS initiative requires every major U.S. military base to sustain operations for 90 days without civilian power or supply chains.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX — The Pentagon is preparing U.S. military bases to keep operating for at least 90 days without outside support as it prepares for the possibility of a major war that could cripple power grids, disrupt supply chains and threaten critical infrastructure on American soil. The new requirement is part of FORTRESS, a broader military initiative aimed at ensuring American forces can continue fighting even if the civilian systems they depend on are disrupted, according to documents reviewed by Fox News Digital. AMERICA'S NEXT WAR COULD REACH US SOIL, TOP ARMY GENERAL WARNS "We don't want to rely on standard civilian municipal infrastructure to run our national defense. We just simply can't. It's an intolerable risk," Pentagon chief spokesperson Sean Parnell told Fox News Digital. The Pentagon is also laying the groundwork for civilian factories to shift to defense production during a crisis, while preparing alternative supply chains and strategic reserves to keep weapons, fuel and other essential materials flowing. "Power is combat now. Without electricity, you lose communications, water, logistics, assembly lines and just basic military command structures," Parnell said. Under FORTRESS, every major military installation in the continental United States would be expected to sustain essential operations independently for at least 90 days, including access to electricity, water, fuel and communications. TRUMP PENTAGON LAUNCHES COMPETITION FOR AMERICA'S NEXT GREAT MILITARY BASE The requirement reflects a broader shift in how the Pentagon is preparing for threats to the American homeland, including the possibility that a major conflict could disrupt the infrastructure supporting military operations inside the United States. "I realized that a lot of the way we think about homeland defense was built around the antiquated assumption that two oceans would protect us," Parnell said. "President Trump understands that world is gone, and he's already paved the way for new thinking: Golden Dome, a renewed focus on the Western Hemisphere, Greenland, Panama." A central concern is the military's reliance on civilian power grids, which support everything from communications and logistics to weapons manufacturing. FORTRESS envisions portable nuclear reactors, large-scale battery storage and microgrids capable of disconnecting military installations from the civilian electrical grid, allowing them to continue operating during prolonged power disruptions. "Mission-critical power must be independent, hardened, and redundant," Parnell said. The Pentagon has already announced plans to reduce major military installations' dependence on civilian power grids. The 90-day self-sufficiency standard goes further, extending the requirement beyond electricity to other essential services needed to sustain military operations. The strategy also anticipates major disruptions to the global supply chains that provide the military with weapons, equipment and critical materials. "The next conflict will likely be fought on multiple fronts. Look at the geopolitics behind any major war. When that happens, global supply chains will break," Parnell said. To prepare, FORTRESS calls for strategic reserves of munitions, fuel, critical minerals, electronics, spare parts and medical supplies that could sustain military operations if international supply routes are disrupted or domestic manufacturers cannot keep pace with wartime demand. Reserve targets would vary depending on how quickly supplies are consumed during a major conflict and how long manufacturers would need to replace them. STARTUPS BRING INNOVATION TO DEFENSE INDUSTRIAL BASE For the military's most critical defense dependencies, the initiative also establishes a requirement for at least two qualified supply or production pathways, reducing the risk that the loss of a single factory, supplier or industrial capability could interrupt military operations. Another major component involves preparing America's civilian manufacturing sector to support a wartime mobilization. Through the Civil Reserve Manufacturing Network, an existing initiative incorporated into FORTRESS, the Pentagon plans to identify commercial factories capable of shifting to defense production during a crisis. The new details describe plans to assess manufacturers' capabilities and establish technical specifications, cybersecurity protections, contracting arrangements and conversion procedures in advance, rather than waiting until a conflict begins. FORTRESS also calls for recurring industrial stress tests and mobilization exercises to assess whether manufacturers could maintain production through prolonged disruptions. Beyond energy and manufacturing, the initiative includes efforts to strengthen military communications, navigation and satellite capabilities against interference, including preparations to maintain operations when GPS signals are jammed or space-based assets are disrupted. Together, the measures are intended to reduce the military's dependence on civilian infrastructure and vulnerable supply networks during a prolonged conflict. "You don't want to be making these decisions in the middle of a global multi-front conflict. We have to have a plan," Parnell said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP He described FORTRESS as an insurance policy for the homeland, designed to ensure American forces can continue operating even if a major war disrupts the infrastructure and supply chains they rely on.

articles.title: Foster children's autism therapy at risk as Georgia lawmakers step into funding fight
articles.summary: Georgia foster children face losing ABA therapy progress after Amerigroup's 30% Medicaid reimbursement cut, as advocates warn clinics may close.
articles.body: A fight over cuts to autism therapy for Georgia foster children is escalating at the state Capitol, with a Republican lawmaker and families now calling for the 30% reimbursement reduction to be reversed as advocates warn children could lose hard-earned progress. State Sen. Brian Strickland, R-McDonough, joined parents and providers Thursday to demand action over a reduction in reimbursement rates for applied behavior analysis (ABA) therapy that went into effect Sept. 1 through Amerigroup, which administers Medicaid coverage for children in Georgia's foster care system. "As a parent of a child with autism, I know what ABA therapy means for a family and Georgia's foster children, which is why I stood at the Capitol to make clear that these cuts are indefensible," Strickland told Fox News Digital. Strickland, who is running for state attorney general, also pledged to hold companies accountable if elected. AUTISM PROVIDERS WARN FOSTER KIDS AT RISK FROM UNINTENDED CONSEQUENCES OF TRUMP'S MEDICAID FRAUD CRACKDOWN The political pushback comes after Fox News Digital first reported earlier this month that autism advocates feared the reduction could force providers to stop treating foster children as an unintended consequence of the Trump administration's Medicaid fraud crackdown. Taylor Sanders of the Autism Families Alliance told Fox News Digital on Saturday that families and clinicians have increasingly begun speaking out since the cuts took effect, emphasizing that "time is crucial to these families." "Every moment where their child is not receiving services, we're seeing a regression in possible communication, safety skills," Sanders said. "Maybe we're seeing an increase in some of those challenging behaviors." Sanders previously warned that as many as 75% of clinics could close or stop serving foster children because of the cuts. AUTISM PROVIDERS CHEER TRUMP CRACKDOWN AFTER MILLIONS ALLEGEDLY STOLEN FROM CHILDREN THROUGH MEDICAID FRAUD She described a family whose 3-year-old child had begun using words for the first time after receiving ABA therapy and whose mother now fears losing access to treatment. "She was in absolute tears and so worried and frustrated," Sanders said, recalling their recent conversation. The mother, Sanders explained, fears losing the consistent one-on-one therapy that she said helped the child begin communicating. Sanders said the child had not received enough therapy to ensure those newly learned communication skills could be maintained across different settings. "For these children and their families, time matters," Kelsey Bennett of the Autism Families Alliance told Fox News Digital. "Every day without critical care risks reversing hard-earned progress and limiting opportunities for continued development." HOUSE GOP BILL MOVES TO CLOSE WHISTLEBLOWER GAPS EXPOSED BY MINNESOTA MEDICAID FRAUD SCANDAL Bennett added, "Reverse the cuts." Advocates are calling not only for the cuts to be reconsidered, but also for families, clinicians and other stakeholders to be involved in reviewing the policy rather than relying on a blanket approach. In a statement to FOX 5 Atlanta, Amerigroup said it rebalanced ABA reimbursement rates based on service complexity and clinical expertise, increasing rates for treatment planning and caregiver-engagement services while decreasing rates for some technician-delivered services. The company also said rates for licensed clinicians did not decrease and that medically necessary autism services remain covered. In response, Sanders emphasized that the reductions affected technicians who provide much of the one-on-one care. COALITION OF 25 STATES SUES TRUMP ADMIN OVER MEDICAID WORK RULE DESIGNED TO PREVENT FRAUD "Just because we put something down on paper doesn't mean that it's gonna be clinically effective or that these children are gonna be able to access care because companies are now having to maybe close their doors to these individuals because they can't afford the rate cut," Sanders said. Sanders reiterated her concerns about the potential long-term consequences for children whose therapy is interrupted. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Progress lost is extremely hard to come back from, which is the biggest concern that we're facing here," Sanders said. "Reconsider before ripping the rug from families. Start to involve the clinicians, involve families before making major cuts." Fox News Digital has reached out to Amerigroup and the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services for additional comment. Fox News Digital's Landon Mion contributed to this report.

articles.title: Mike Johnson's future hangs in balance as the 'accidental speaker' marks 3 years
articles.summary: Mike Johnson marks three years as House Speaker with $526 million in fundraising, but the midterm elections could threaten the Republican majority.
articles.body: Three years ago today marked the end of one of the most chaotic periods in American political history. Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., took control of the House of Representatives after a unanimous vote by his fellow Republicans, ending three weeks of paralysis in the federal government. His predecessor, Kevin McCarthy, had been ousted by GOP rebels in the first such rebellion against a sitting House speaker in U.S. history. The Louisiana Republican, having served in Congress only since 2017, surprised his peers and the country with his rapid ascent to power. And since then, Johnson — who has been dubbed the "accidental speaker" by multiple parties — has made a name for himself as one of the most effective speakers the House has seen, given his razor-thin majority. But the third anniversary of his speakership comes just over a week before an election that could see Johnson lose it all — despite his best efforts to defy history and keep the House GOP in power. JOHNSON DELIVERS BIG FOR TRUMP, BUT FRUSTRATION GROWS ACROSS RAZOR-THIN GOP MAJORITY "Over the last three years — in spite of the constant challenges governing with one of the smallest majorities in history — House Republicans have delivered landmark victories for the American people," Johnson told Fox News Digital. "We enacted the largest tax cuts for hardworking families in U.S. history, added 1 million private sector jobs, cut $1.6 trillion in wasteful spending, secured the border, reversed outrageous Biden-era regulations, achieved the lowest violent crime rate in 126 years and the largest decline in prescription drug prices in 60 years," he said. "We created Trump accounts for every child and the first nationwide school choice program, voted to ban stock trading in Congress, passed landmark housing legislation, and so much more." JOHNSON TURNS DEMOCRATS’ SOCIALIST CIVIL WAR INTO NEW WEAPON FOR MIDTERMS He’s done much of that with a majority fluctuating between one and four seats, a remarkably tight margin during a tenure that Newt Gingrich called "the most challenging speakership since the Civil War." Johnson also touted breaking fundraising records and his work "endlessly" traveling the country campaigning for other GOP candidates. MIKE JOHNSON TAUNTS HAKEEM JEFFRIES FOR LOSING DEMS' CIVIL WAR 'IN HIS OWN BACKYARD' "I remain grateful every day to my colleagues for their continued confidence as we fight together to protect our House majority. Serving as their 56th Speaker of the House is the honor of my life," he said. In his three years, Johnson has already become one of the GOP’s most prolific fundraisers in history. He’s raised $526 million for Republicans during this election cycle alone. The month before Election Day, Johnson campaigned in more than 40 districts across 22 states, and of his 55 endorsed candidates, 97% won their respective primaries. But the million-dollar question is: Is it enough come Nov. 3? House Republicans are facing significant headwinds in their quest to keep the majority. Political convention dictates that the president’s party traditionally loses control of Congress during the midterms, and President Donald Trump’s low approval numbers are expected to complicate matters for Republicans in tight races across the country. Johnson, for his part, has remained optimistic but has tried not to give any hints about what he would do if the GOP lost. REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: CONGRESS BRACES FOR POST-ELECTION GAME OF MUSICAL CHAIRS AS LEADERSHIP BATTLES LOOM "Heaven forbid, if we lose this majority or whatever, I don’t know what my next chapter of life is," Johnson told Fox News' Aishah Hasnie this month. "If God moves on our hearts and says we should, you know, go back to my hometown of Shreveport and start a lawn business, I’ll do that with equal fervor." Days later he told CBS News, "I don't think it's going to happen, so I don't spend any time thinking about it ... But in the unlikely scenario where we lost the majority, I would expect my colleagues would ask me to continue leading this conference, even if we have divided government." Whether Johnson’s fellow House Republicans even want him to stay will come down to how well Republicans do, and if they lose, how bad that loss will be. Multiple GOP lawmakers who spoke with Fox News Digital earlier this month said they anticipated Johnson would step aside if Republicans lost the House. If they win, however, Johnson is all but assured of keeping his job — and with Trump’s blessing. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Speaker Mike Johnson is an example of the American Dream. As Speaker, he's continued to defy the odds with a slim House majority and pass America First bills," Trump’s campaign posted on X. "After Republicans win in November, they should re-elect Mike as Speaker quickly!"

articles.title: Scaramucci compares Ramaswamy to pigs in ‘Animal Farm,’ predicts loss
articles.summary: Former White House communications director Anthony Scaramucci on Sunday compared Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy (R) to the pig characters in the George Orwell novel “Animal Farm” and predicted that the candidate will lose to opponent Amy Acton (D). “Vivek Ramswamy has disgraced himself,” Scaramucci wrote on the social platform X. “Ramaswamy started with soaring…
articles.body:
Former White House communications director Anthony Scaramucci on Sunday compared Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy (R) to the pig characters in the George Orwell novel “Animal Farm” and predicted that the candidate will lose to opponent Amy Acton (D).

“Vivek Ramswamy has disgraced himself,” Scaramucci wrote on the social platform X . “Ramaswamy started with soaring rhetoric, post-partisan, data-dependent, technology entrepreneur, here to bring good government to the American people.”

“But like the pigs at the end of ‘Animal Farm’: they despised the two-legged farmers, by the last chapter they’re living in the house, up on their hind legs, little vests on, pocket watches,” he continued. “They became exactly what they abhorred. That’s what happened here. In order to win, politicians break their first principles. They abandon their righteous philosophies and sink into a scum position. Ramaswamy did that to himself.”

Scaramucci’s post concludes by predicting that the Ohio Republican will lose “and I think he’s finished himself as a future candidate.”

Orwell’s novella, published in 1945, depicts a satirical analogue of the Russian Revolution, where farm animals rise up to take control away from their human masters and create a dictatorial system of fear resembling the Soviet Union under Joseph Stalin.

Ramaswamy has faced uproar in recent days after spending $4 million to broadcast a campaign ad featuring Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur, accusing the Democrat of being a “liar” her whole life.

Acton was removed from her mother’s custody at age 12 after her stepfather was charged with sexually abusing her. Arthur remained with Acton’s stepfather until his death.

Acton herself called the ad “ despicable ” and added it was “an exploitative thing to do.”

Ohio Republicans like Gov. Mike DeWine (R) and his predecessor John Kasich (R) have called on Ramaswamy’s campaign to have the ad pulled. Conservative commentator Scott Jennings, an ally of President Trump who frequently defends the president and the GOP, slammed the ad and told CNN’s Anderson Cooper that it was “not good” morally and was a political misstep.

Ramaswamy took credit for the ad, doubled down on it and accused Acton of “lying about an ad that is about lying.”

The candidate’s strongest defenders have been Trump and Vice President Vance, with Trump saying he trusts Acton’s mother. Both slammed Ohio Republicans over their criticism of the ad.

“[DeWine] strongly suggested that Vivek should, ‘take down the Ad,'” Trump wrote on Truth Social last Thursday . “He probably wants a Dumocrat to win, and certainly doesn’t want someone who will do a much better job than he is capable of doing. I suggested, on the other hand, that Vivek should keep it up.”

Vance said during a fraud task force press conference on Wednesday that he was “a little bit disgusted” by Republicans “whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America.”

articles.title: Trump fails to change economic headwinds facing GOP candidates
articles.summary: Gas, diesel and food prices are high and expected to remain elevated through Election Day, creating a strong political headwind for Republicans who are at serious risk of losing control of the House and possibly the Senate, as well. President Trump’s diesel deal with Russia has had little lasting impact on fuel prices, according to…
articles.body:
Gas, diesel and food prices are high and expected to remain elevated through Election Day, creating a strong political headwind for Republicans who are at serious risk of losing control of the House and possibly the Senate , as well.

President Trump’s diesel deal with Russia has had little lasting impact on fuel prices , according to economic experts. The national average price of diesel stood at $6.28 a gallon on Friday, significantly higher than where it was before Trump launched strikes against Iran, which was $3.72 per gallon in February.

High fuel prices have pushed up food prices, despite Trump’s interventions to control costs across the U.S. economy.

The price of ground beef is now hovering around $6.80 a pound despite Trump’s order in August to import 300,000 metric tons of foreign beef.

Consumer borrowing rates are high, including the rate for a 30-year fixed mortgage, which stands at 7.32 percent.

Congress passed the 21st Century Road to Housing Act in July but it has had little impact on the worst housing market in years.

Pending home sales dropped 7.3 percent from August to September, representing an 11.3 percent year-over-year decline, according to the National Association of Realtors.

Recognizing the gravity of the housing affordability crisis, Trump on Thursday signed an executive order to lower insurance premiums, refinancing costs and interest rates on some government-backed home loans, but it’s unlikely to have much impact before Nov. 3.

It adds up to an economic environment that has put voters in a sour mood and gives Democrats a chance to capture Senate seats even in Republican-leaning states such as Alaska, Iowa, Kansas and Texas.

“The economists tell us the economy is doing well, there are a lot of great numbers for the Trump administration but the bottom line is Americans aren’t feeling it. Many Americans feel like their dollars aren’t going as far. They’re paying higher prices for gas, higher prices for groceries,” said Brian Darling, a Republican strategist.

Darling said Trump’s diesel deal with Russian hasn’t had much of an impact on fuel prices.

“Diesel prices are really high and that is the most extreme energy inflation that we’re seeing in the economy right now,” he said.

He warned that if “gas prices creep up right up to Election Day, that’s bad news for Republicans.”

“That is something that’s been a real problem for Republicans,” he said. “If they go up between now and Election Day, that may be a tiebreaker in many of these close races.”

Trump on Thursday announced that he would invoke the Defense Production Act to boost domestic oil production and refining capacity.

The announcement came a few weeks after Trump shocked Republican senators by announcing a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import hundreds of thousands of tons of Russian diesel into the United States.

But economic experts say Trump’s deal with Russia and his recent invocation of the Defense Production Act will hardly impact prices before Election Day.

“Gas prices are not going to come down until we have an end to the war” with Iran and there’s a “ramp-up of production and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz,” said Neale Mahoney, a professor of economics at Stanford University.

He noted that Trump’s negotiations with Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz have “been largely going sideways over the last few weeks” and predicted, “I don’t expect any sharp deviations from that trend.”

The price of brent crude oil rose to a six-month high on Friday, gaining more than 3 percent to close at $116 a barrel.

West Texas Intermediate, the other oil benchmark, rose nearly 4 percent to close at $103 a barrel Friday.

That in turn is putting upward pressure on food prices, say experts.

“Diesel prices and also the reduced exports of fertilizer out of the Strait of Hormuz impact the economy over time,” Mahoney said. “Over time, the increase of the price of fertilizer works its way through into agricultural prices.

“We expect to see higher agricultural prices heading into the rest of the fall and the winter, combined with El Niño, which is going to strain global food supply,” he warned, referring to the increase in ocean temperatures in the Pacific that are expected to impact weather patterns over the next several months.

“Those two shocks together are going to put increased strain on food prices. Gas and food are the prices that consumers see most often,” he added. “They’re the ones in polling and in focus groups that [people] say they are the most frustrated about.”

Political and policy experts say the relentless rise in prices have fueled growing public pessimism over the U.S. economy and voter anger over Trump’s management of the economy.

The University of Michigan’s Surveys of Consumers reported on Friday that U.S. consumer sentiment dropped to near a record low in October, the second-lowest reading on record after the one set in May. Consumers are 15 percent less optimistic about the economy than they were in February, before the war in Iran sent oil prices soaring.

The latest CNBC All-America Economic Survey of 1,000 registered voters published on Thursday found that 8 out of 10 Americans rate the economy as fair or poor and that 35 percent of Republicans say they are pessimistic about the economy.

The poll found that only 33 percent of voters approve of Trump’s handling of the economy while 63 percent disapprove.

Trump has stepped up his efforts in recent weeks to change voters’ views by taking decisive action to address costs, such as announcing an $8 billion relief program to help farmers afford diesel costs during harvest season.

The president is also taking credit for new investments coming to battlegrounds states, such as the $15 billion Mesabi Metallics steel plant that he announced would be build in Iowa, creating 1,750 new jobs.

But political and policy experts say that voters’ negative views of the economy are mostly baked in and that Trump’s actions to address the affordability crisis, something he dismissed as a “hoax” in December, aren’t likely to change many people’s minds.

“They are too little, too late. It’s not clear that any of these initiatives are going to bring prices down,” said Darrell West, a senior fellow in the governance studies program at the Brookings Institution.

“People are worried housing, healthcare, child care and other issues and his moves don’t meaningfully reduce the cost of living for people,” he said.

“He hasn’t manage to bring down beef costs even though he has made some deals. The problem is that many things he’s done hasn’t addressed the fundamental problem,” he added, referring to Trump. “The Iran war has raised fuel prices and the cost of manufactured goods.

“There are many sectors where there are only two, three or four companies so we don’t really have meaningful price competition. There are just big structural issues he hasn’t addressed,” West said.

Darling, the GOP strategist, said Trump is working hard to show voters that he’s laser-focused on the economy but acknowledged the president’s failure to end the conflict with Iran continues to be a big political problem for Republicans because voters blame rising costs on the war.

“President Trump is working hard to make the rounds, do rallies, trying to cut deals to make the economy a little bit better. But the bottom line is that for the economy to change, that takes a long period of time,” he said.

He called the military conflict with Iran “the most important issue.”

“The Iran war is impacting gas prices, grocery prices. And a lot of Republicans supported the president because he wasn’t going to start any new wars. They’re disillusioned,” he said.

articles.title: The myth of special treatment for undocumented immigrant college students
articles.summary: Undocumented immigrants are taxpayers. Why shouldn’t their children, for whom they have often sacrificed so much, enjoy the benefits their parents have worked to earn?
articles.body:
At the high school where I teach, this time of year is always a little awkward.

Our college-bound seniors are creating their Free Application for Federal Student Aid accounts and beginning the process of collecting information and documentation to meet the December deadline. The students, many of whom have been together for four years or more, must now sort themselves into two categories: Americans and “illegals.” The U.S. citizens apply for FAFSA. The undocumented students cannot; they must fill out the California Dream Act Application instead.

It is also at this time of year that a few students get some very unwelcome news — they were not born here, but were brought here when they were very young. Their parents never told them, perhaps not wanting to burden their children, or out of embarrassment, or believing that by the time their kids graduated the immigration mess would be sorted out. These students are not citizens like their classmates; they’re not even green card holders. They have no legal right to be here.

If the Trump administration has its way, many of these will not be able to go to college.

The Department of Justice recently filed the last of 25 lawsuits against states that make undocumented students eligible for in-state tuition. These lawsuits have already succeeded in Illinois, Texas, Oklahoma, Nebraska, Kentucky and Kansas.

As Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward Jr. explains, “Illegal aliens will not receive benefits denied to American citizens.” And Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate of the Justice Department’s civil division says, “This Department of Justice will not tolerate American students being treated like second-class citizens in their own country.”

Many on the right support the Justice Department’s actions. The New York Post describes California’s tuition system as the state “paying tens of millions of dollars for illegal immigrants to attend college — infuriating Golden State natives struggling to pay their tuition.” California Republican gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton says he will cut state-funded aid for undocumented students.

A recent California Post cover story , “World Class Welfare: Migrants get aid while California kids struggle,” features two 21-year-old California college seniors who are struggling to pay for college. Rather than attend one of the state’s many public universities, they chose to go to private colleges with yearly tuition of $70K or more. Yet both still find a way to blame immigrants. One explains, “I felt like I did all the work to earn my spot in this school and yet I’m the one that’s not getting aid, and undocumented illegal aliens are instead getting that money.”

The case for offering undocumented students in-state tuition and state financial aid is a sound one. Undocumented immigrants pay a wide variety of state taxes, including sales tax, state income tax, gasoline tax, and property taxes through their rents.

There are roughly 525,000 undocumented college students in the U.S., and California, with 102,000, has the most. In so-called “Taxifornia,” everyone, including the undocumented, pay the highest sales taxes and gasoline taxes in the country. For low-income workers, both of these taxes are highly regressive.

Most undocumented workers also pay California’s income tax, which is also the highest in the country.

In addition, according to the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy, undocumented immigrants pay nearly $26 billion per year in Social Security taxes , even though most will likely never receive Social Security benefits.

In the University of California system, students paying in-state tuition are charged $15,588 per year instead of $54,858. In-state tuition for California State University students for two 12-unit semesters is $6,838, as opposed to $11,304 for out-of-state.

According to Sallie Mae, in-state tuition is lower because “residents are already supporting state schools when they pay their state taxes, so they’ve earned a discount.” This precept is hardly new. When the University of California was founded in 1868, and for a century afterward, tuition was free for California residents.

Undocumented students aren’t getting “benefits denied to American citizens” — out-of-state students are not and never have been eligible for in-state tuition.

Longtime California political strategist Jon Fleischman condemns California for “decid[ing] that being in the country illegally should not stand in the way of getting help from California taxpayers to pay for college.”

But undocumented immigrants are taxpayers. Why shouldn’t their children, for whom they have often sacrificed so much, enjoy the benefits their parents have worked to earn?

Glenn Sacks teaches social studies at James Monroe High School in the Los Angeles Unified School District. His columns on education and politics have appeared in many of America’s largest publications .
